input: Compare naive RAG vs sentence-window retrieval
expected_output: Naive RAG splits documents into fixed-size chunks without considering sentence boundaries, which can break context mid-sentence and hurt retrieval quality. Sentence-window retrieval instead identifies the most relevant sentence and returns a surrounding window of sentences, preserving local context. Sentence-window retrieval generally achieves better precision and coherence in answers because each retrieved chunk is semantically self-contained.

input: What are best practices for chunking documents in RAG systems?
expected_output: Best practices for chunking in RAG include: choosing chunk sizes between 256-512 tokens for general text; using sentence-aware or paragraph-aware splitting rather than fixed character counts; adding overlap between adjacent chunks (10-20%) to preserve cross-chunk context; storing metadata (source, page, section) with each chunk; experimenting with different chunk sizes and evaluating retrieval quality empirically.

input: How does hybrid search (BM25 + vector) improve retrieval quality?
expected_output: Hybrid search combines BM25 (sparse keyword-based retrieval) and dense vector (semantic similarity) retrieval. BM25 excels at exact keyword matches and rare terms, while vector search handles semantic similarity and synonyms. Their combination via an ensemble retriever with weighted scores captures both lexical precision and semantic understanding, typically outperforming either method alone. Cross-encoder reranking can further refine the combined results.

input: What embedding models work best for scientific document retrieval?
expected_output: For scientific document retrieval, domain-specific models like SPECTER2, SciBERT, and BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 tend to outperform general-purpose embeddings. BAAI/bge models are strong general retrievers that also perform well on scientific text. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large offers high quality but at a cost. The best choice depends on domain specificity, language, and latency requirements.

input: Explain the role of cross-encoder reranking in RAG pipelines
expected_output: Cross-encoder reranking is a two-stage refinement step in RAG pipelines. After initial retrieval (by BM25 or vector search) returns a candidate set, a cross-encoder model scores each query-document pair jointly, enabling much finer relevance judgments than bi-encoders allow. Models like BAAI/bge-reranker-base evaluate the full interaction between query and passage, reordering candidates by true relevance. This typically improves answer quality at the cost of added latency.

input: What is the optimal chunk size for a 1-paragraph legal contract clause in Ukrainian?
expected_output: For a single-paragraph legal clause in Ukrainian, a chunk size of 128-256 tokens is usually appropriate to keep the clause intact. Legal text benefits from semantic splitting at clause boundaries rather than arbitrary token limits. Overlap is less critical for short clauses. Ukrainian text may require a tokenizer aware of Cyrillic script.

input: Is RAG better than fine-tuning for production LLM applications?
expected_output: Neither RAG nor fine-tuning is universally better; it depends on the use case. RAG is preferred when the knowledge base changes frequently, when citations are required, or when data privacy prevents sending documents to a model. Fine-tuning is better for changing model style, behavior, or learning domain-specific reasoning patterns. Many production systems combine both approaches.
